content.thinking:
I need to write the whole file carefully in one pass without testing, keeping it correct against the API. I'm designing a red panda on a mossy stone at realistic scale—roughly 0.6m body, 0.5m tail, 0.25m standing height on all fours—with the stone around 0.4m wide and 0.3m tall, keeping all four legs planted on the rock in a neutral balanced pose.

Now I'm working out the exact geometry: the stone as a squashed sphere with mottled moss coloring, positioned so its top surface sits near y=0.27, then calculating where the panda's hips, shoulders, and paws need to land on that curved surface using the ellipsoid equation to make sure each foot touches the rock correctly at its specific x/z offset.

Working out the spine curve and hip positioning, then sizing the limb segments so hind and front legs reach their foot targets with enough slack to bend naturally at the knee and elbow.

Placing the hips joint as root facing forward, then working out the spine chain up to the neck and adding a separate head joint aimed forward, extending the body sweep path to end near the neck so the head attaches cleanly at the top.

For the head itself, I'm picturing a wide round red panda skull with a small pointed snout and large triangular ears, positioning the head joint and building a skull sphere scaled to the right proportions, using absolute coordinates tied to the head bone rather than local frames to keep things simple.

Still working out the facial features... cheek tufts as outward-pointing spikes, a cream-colored snout sphere, a tiny dark nose, and a separate jaw piece with its own bone joint for mouth articulation, before moving on to placing the eye decals on the skull.

Writing face paint function...

Still working out the ear geometry...

Simpler fix: make the inner ear layer just slightly thicker than the outer at the same center, so it naturally pokes through on both faces without worrying about sign conventions. Now moving on to fur tufts — planning a flame-shaped SVG texture for the tuft cards.

For color, the greyscale tuft texture gets tinted by the part's paint, so I can use a plain white/grey drawing and let the material tint handle the coloring. Next I'm working out the actual palette: a rust-red/orange back, dark plum belly and legs, and ringed tail coloring to match a red-panda-meets-Genshin aesthetic.

Writing fur paint coat logic...

Now defining dark leg paint and sweeping each leg as a tapered chain, placing front shoulders/feet and hind hip/feet coordinates symmetrically on both sides.

I'm working out limb attachment points to spine joints—hind legs parenting to joint 0, front legs to joint 2—and setting bend hints so the hind knees angle forward and the front elbows angle backward.

Each paw gets a small flattened sphere positioned at the ankle's tip joint, scaled to sit right at the stone surface height, plus a few tiny toe spheres per foot for added detail colored dark plum with cream claw tips.

Now I'm working out the tail as a bushy chain hanging back from the hips and curving upward in an S-shape above the stone, with radii tapering then flaring out toward a bushy tip, naming each segment tail1 through tail5.

For coloring, I'm applying alternating darker rust-red stripe bands along the tail using a cel-shaded stripe pattern, then adding a gradient so the tip darkens toward a plum-black color for a realistic ringed tail look.

Now I'm scattering fur cards along the tail with tuft tinting, then adding denser fur cards across the body (around 220 instances) filtered to avoid the underside, tinted by the coat paint color read at each card's root. Next I'm setting up cheek tuft spikes.

For whiskers I'll use thin cream rods with few sides for efficiency. Then for the stone material, I'm blending moss green patches onto grey-blue rock using noise-based height masking so moss appears more on upper, flatter surfaces.

Writing paint function...

Now I'm thinking about adding decorative details on the stone—moss tufts rendered as colored cards, plus small flowers and mushrooms. I'll build mushrooms from a cone and sphere cap, coloring the cap pink with cream spots using the paint function, and place them stuck into the stone edge via hit detection.

Instead of relying on scattered hits, I'm deciding to place mushrooms manually by casting downward rays at specific x,z coordinates onto the stone surface to find valid sticking points. I'm also working through the rigging logic—figuring out whether the stone should attach to the "hips" bone, or whether I need a separate root joint for the stone so it doesn't awkwardly follow the panda's hip movement.

Settling on the joint hierarchy: stone becomes the root joint, with hips parenting off it, and the panda parented to hips. Now I'm sketching out the full joint list—spine chain, head, jaw, ears (adding separate earL/earR joints so they can move independently), tail, and legs—while assigning roles like "spine", "tail", "leg", "head", and "jaw" to keep everything under the part budget.

Thinking through pose details now: I want the tail arched upward in a graceful S-curve for a balancing effect, head tilted slightly down-forward as if looking at something, and all four paws planted on the stone. I'm adjusting the tail curve points so the tip rises to about 0.85-0.88 overall height without clipping into the body, keeping the stone's bottom sphere resting right at floor level.

I'm checking proportions next -- the torso path and radii tapering from hips to chest to neck, and I'm noticing the legs may be coming out too short relative to the body, since red pandas have visibly longer legs than what's currently showing between the hip joint and the feet.

Now I'm recalculating the paint thresholds for the skull, figuring out where the white marking starts and placing the eye positions based on the skull's radius and angle, since the decals need to project correctly onto the curved surface.

Refining face coloring logic...

Working out the ear extrusion frame...

Defining ear outline points...

Now checking the ear base placement relative to the skull and setting up the joint rig, then working through how eye decals get placed using surface hits with azimuth/elevation lookups and tint rotation per side before moving to eyebrow marks and stone detail parts.

I'm sizing the main stone and surrounding pebbles with low-poly flat faceting, making sure none of the smaller stones poke above or below the main stone's vertical bounds near the base.

Checking paw placement against the stone's curved surface, I'm computing the sunk depth at hind and front positions to confirm the paws rest slightly embedded rather than floating. I'm also accounting for the sphere's low segment count, since the faceted top sits a bit lower than the ideal smooth curve, so I'm recalculating the actual ring height using the facet angle to get an accurate surface position.

I'll derive an approximate stone-surface height function to place mushrooms near the edges, computing sunk stem positions for three red spotted mushroom caps, and plan moss cards scattered across the surface filtered by upward-facing normals.

For the stone part I'll register it as a surface for hit detection, then design simple SVG textures: a moss tuft with green blade shapes, a lighter fur-like tuft texture, and tiny flowers made from small spheres arranged in a ring around a yellow center to sit on the stone.

I'm also thinking about adding a gold accent detail, like a small collar with a glowing teal charm hanging at the neck, trying to figure out the best way to position a ring geometry around the neck joint without risking errors from missing bones.

Adding the gem glow and tassel threads hanging below the pendant, attaching them to the nearest spine joint with a teal glow color for the gem.

I'm also scattering small floating teal motes around the stone to suggest a dendro-elemental sparkle, keeping them under the height limit, then defining the head joint position and setting up the spine chain naming convention.

Adding the hips and tail joints next, making sure parent references and names stay distinct, before moving to the body sweep operation...

For fur painting I'm using a cel-shaded edge function with a normal-based belly darkening threshold, plus a reddish chest patch typical of red pandas, and defining a smooth five-point radius profile for the body. For the legs I'm picking a dark brown-black color for the main leg shading with rustier tones near the hips, and planning lighter paw tips.

Adding cream claws and pads to each paw, computing toe positions and small claw spikes per toe for a total of twenty-four tiny parts, then setting up whisker rods extending from the snout sides at varying angles and lengths.

Now I'm scattering fur cards across the body surface using a filtered random distribution, orienting and bending them with some size and lean variation to mimic orange mottled fur, then switching the texture palette to greyscale with white flame shapes and grey line details.

For the tail and head I'm placing separate card scatters—coarser tail coat cards and finer cream cheek-ruff cards on the skull, filtering by position so they wrap naturally around ears and cheeks. I'm also finalizing the export metadata (name, description, Genshin Impact style tag, commit hash) and making sure only the actually-used type imports are included to avoid lint errors.

Now I'm setting up the builder and defining the color palette—oranges, rust, cream, plum, gold—then composing the coat paints using mottled cel-shaded gradients and a fur-edge toothed transition between light and dark fur, plus a striped paint for the tail.

Still writing color and face paint logic...

Still refining cheek shading logic...

For the mushroom, I'm designing the stem as a small tapered cylinder in a cream tone, with the cap as a flattened sphere colored in pink with cream spots, wrapped in a cel-shaded spots paint for a toon look.

Now I'm checking mushroom placements against the stone's ellipse boundary and the panda's leg positions to make sure nothing overlaps, then setting flower positions that stay clear of the panda's body and legs.

Writing flower stem geometry...

I'm also placing floating glowing motes around the scene and a pendant gem glow, plus adding moss tuft cards onto the stone surface using tinted textures.

Scattering mushroom and moss cards across the stone, avoiding the panda's feet area, with random lean and spin for natural variation. I'm also adding a few flat pebble pieces glued onto the stone using icosahedron shapes with rock paint applied.

Now I'm setting up the eye texture with amber iris and pink blush, deciding to keep anime-style brows for a cleaner look rather than literal red panda markings. I'm positioning the eyes around the skull center and adding a gold torus collar near the neck, checking it against the spine and torso radius so it sits properly without clipping.

Adding small gold sphere details ringed around the collar for extra ornamentation, using a ring helper tied to the spine joint frame so the decorations follow the neck bone.

Now I'm adding tassel threads hanging from the gem — three thin red rods angled outward from the gem position, plus a small gold bead accent. Then I'm building out the skull shape using a scaled sphere geometry positioned at the head, bound to the head bone for proper deformation.

Writing whiskers and ruff spikes...

I'm placing the jaw sphere so it tucks under the snout with the mouth closed, skipping extra details like the tongue or mouth line for simplicity. For the ears, I'll treat their joints as hinge roles, and confirm the leg chain can take an array of points for its sweep path since the limb function returns a Vector3 array that fits the expected polyline input.

Now I'm positioning the leg sockets so they stay inside the body silhouette — shoulders near the body radius at that depth, hips tucked under the belly curve — then working out foot placement and segment lengths so the bend geometry actually resolves to something plausible. I'm naming the chain joints per side (hip/knee/ankle for hind legs, shoulder/elbow/wrist for front) with a left/right suffix to keep them distinct.

Next I'm sketching the paw geometry — small flattened spheres colored and positioned at each foot bone tip — then writing out the scatter logic for the moss/stone decoration, with a filter to exclude spots too close to the paws so the feet stay unobstructed.
